summary: Describes an extension to IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration under which hosts generate temporary addresses with randomized interface identifiers. Changing addresses over time limits how long eavesdroppers and others can use the address to track a device.

plainLanguage.summary: When an IPv6 device sets up its own address, this document makes the device create an extra address whose last part is random, and to replace it with a new random one every day or so. Because the number changes, an observer cannot easily tell that two unrelated conversations came from the same device.

questions: how long do ipv6 temporary addresses last
how are temporary ipv6 interface identifiers generated
why does each ipv6 prefix need a different temporary address
subtitle: How an IPv6 host keeps a changing, random part in its address so the same identifier is not reused for every connection.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses built by stateless autoconfiguration usually keep the same interface identifier for as long as the host is on the network, so anyone who can see the addresses can tell that several unrelated transactions came from one device.
tldr.mechanism: The host creates a temporary address for each prefix it is offered, built from a randomized interface identifier, and replaces it with a fresh one before it expires. Each address gets its own random lifetime offset so that many hosts do not all change at the same moment.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8981 obsoletes RFC 4941. It replaces the MD5-based identifier with a pseudorandom generator or a keyed function, gives each prefix its own identifier, and shortens the default valid lifetime from one week to two days.

today: RFC 8981 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4941, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its default maximum valid lifetime for temporary addresses is two days.

sections.title: Temporary Addresses for Autoconfigured Hosts
sections.content:
RFC 4862 specifies Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) for IPv6, which typically results in hosts configuring one or more stable IPv6 addresses. Each of them is composed of a network prefix advertised by a local router and a locally generated interface identifier (IID).

This document specifies an extension to SLAAC that causes hosts to generate temporary addresses with randomized interface identifiers for each prefix advertised with autoconfiguration enabled. Changing addresses over time limits the window during which eavesdroppers and other information collectors can trivially perform address-based network-activity correlation when the same address is used for multiple transactions by the same host. It also reduces the window of exposure of a host as being accessible via an address that becomes revealed as a result of active communication.

The default address selection for IPv6 is specified in RFC 6724. In some cases the decision between stable and temporary addresses can only be made by an application, and an Application Programming Interface such as the one in RFC 5014 can let individual applications indicate a preference.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal autoconfigured IPv6 address has a fixed part that comes from the router and a fixed part that the device makes up. This document keeps that address and adds a second one whose second half is random, so the device does not use the same identifier for everything it does.

sections.title: One Identifier, Many Transactions
sections.content:
Addresses generated using SLAAC contain an embedded interface identifier that may remain stable over time. Anytime a fixed identifier is used in multiple contexts, it becomes possible to correlate seemingly unrelated activity using it. The correlation can be performed by an attacker on the path between the host and its peers, who can see the IPv6 addresses in the datagrams, or by an attacker who can access the communication logs of those peers.

Because the identifier is embedded in the IPv6 address, it cannot be hidden. Even when higher layers encrypt their payloads, addresses in packet headers appear in the clear. If a mobile host accesses the network from several locations, an eavesdropper might therefore track its movement from place to place even when the payloads are encrypted.

An attacker on the path may still correlate on the payload contents of unencrypted packets, or on characteristics such as packet size and timing. Use of temporary addresses does not prevent that, and it does not prevent an on-link observer such as the host's default router from tracking all of the host's addresses. The network prefix is a constant identifier too: all hosts at a home share one, so if a network holds only a single host, changing just the interface identifier does not improve privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason for the change is that addresses are visible in every packet. A watcher who records them can group together everything one device did, even when the contents are encrypted. Randomizing the last part of the address breaks that grouping, although it does not hide traffic patterns or stop the local router from seeing every address.

sections.title: Design Guidelines for Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
Temporary addresses observe six properties. They are typically employed for initiating outgoing sessions. They are used for a short period of time, typically hours to days, and are subsequently deprecated; deprecated addresses can continue to be used for established connections but are not used to initiate new connections. New temporary addresses are generated over time to replace expired ones. They must have a limited lifetime, both a valid lifetime and a preferred lifetime, and that lifetime should be reduced further when privacy-meaningful events take place, such as the host attaching to a different network or regenerating a randomized Media Access Control (MAC) address. The lifetime of temporary addresses must be statistically different for different addresses, so that it is hard to predict when a new one is generated or to correlate a new one with an existing one.

By default, one address is generated for each prefix advertised by SLAAC, and the resulting interface identifiers must be statistically different for different prefixes and different network interfaces. It must be difficult for an outside entity to predict the identifiers that will be used, even with knowledge of the algorithm used to generate them and of the identifiers used before. These identifiers must be semantically opaque and must not follow any specific patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: A temporary address is short-lived, meant for starting outgoing connections, and then set aside but left usable for connections already open. Each address gets a slightly different lifetime, so hosts do not all replace their address at the same time, and every prefix and every network card gets its own random identifier.

sections.title: Generating a Randomized Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The document gives two example algorithms. The first assumes a pseudorandom number generator is available. The host obtains a random number with at least as many bits as the identifier needs, takes as many bits from it as necessary, and compares the result against the reserved IPv6 interface identifiers and against identifiers already used on the same interface and prefix. If the identifier is unacceptable, the algorithm is repeated from the first step.

The second algorithm augments the one in RFC 7217, so a host can use a single algorithm for stable and temporary addresses by choosing the right parameters. The host computes a random identifier with the expression shown below, where F is a pseudorandom function that cannot be computed from outside without the secret key and is difficult to reverse, and should produce at least as many bits as the identifier needs. BLAKE3 with a 256-bit key and arbitrary-length output is one possible option, and a keyed-hash message authentication code is another, with HMAC-SHA-256 named as a possible implementation. The use of HMAC-MD5 is considered unacceptable.

The inputs are the prefix learned from an ICMPv6 Router Advertisement, the MAC address of the network interface card, a network identifier such as the IEEE 802.11 Service Set Identifier, a representation of time, a counter used to resolve conflicts, and a secret key that is not known by the attacker. The secret key should be at least 128 bits, must be initialized to a pseudorandom number when the operating system is bootstrapped, and must not be used for any other purpose, such as generating stable addresses. The identifier is finally obtained by taking as many bits from the computed value as necessary, starting from the least significant bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Two methods are given. The simple one draws a random number and cuts it to size. The other feeds several inputs, including a secret key held by the device, into a keyed function, which produces a value that cannot be reproduced without that key. The result is checked against reserved and already-used identifiers and drawn again if it clashes.

sections.title: Creating and Replacing Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
When a host processes a Router Advertisement with a Prefix Information option carrying a prefix for address autoconfiguration, it adjusts the lifetimes of its existing temporary addresses, with the constraint that no temporary address stays valid or preferred longer than TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME or TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus DESYNC_FACTOR. If the host has not configured a temporary address for that prefix, it should create one. When creating an address, the host computes a DESYNC_FACTOR, takes the lower of the prefix's valid lifetime and TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME as the valid lifetime, and the lower of the prefix's preferred lifetime and TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus DESYNC_FACTOR as the preferred lifetime. An address is created only if the calculated preferred lifetime is greater than REGEN_ADVANCE, and an address with a zero preferred lifetime must not be created.

The new address is made by appending a randomized identifier to the received prefix. The host then performs Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) on it. If DAD shows the address is already in use, the host generates a new identifier and repeats, up to TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES times. After that many consecutive failures the host must log a system error and should not try again for that prefix for the duration of its attachment to the network through that interface.

When a temporary address becomes deprecated, a new one must be generated, except when the deprecation was caused by a Prefix Information option with a zero preferred lifetime, in which case no new address may be generated in response to that same option. A new address should be regenerated slightly before its predecessor is deprecated, and the host should start that process REGEN_ADVANCE time units before deprecation. When an interface connects to a new link, existing temporary addresses for that interface must be removed and new ones generated, so that the two links use different identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: When the router offers a prefix, the host makes one temporary address for it, checks that the address is not already taken, and repeats if it is. When an address reaches the end of its preferred lifetime the host builds a replacement, starting the work early enough that the new address is ready in time. Moving to a new network replaces all of the host's temporary addresses.

sections.title: Lifetimes, Timers and Randomization
sections.content:
The document defines five parameters. TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME has a default of 2 days and users should be able to override it. TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME has a default of 1 day, users should be able to override it, and it must be smaller than TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME to avoid the pathological case where an address is used for new communications but becomes invalid in less than one second. REGEN_ADVANCE is 2 + (TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES * DupAddrDetectTransmits * RetransTimer / 1000), expressed in seconds, which accounts for the time possibly spent in DAD in the worst case. MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR is 0.4 * TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME, the upper bound on DESYNC_FACTOR, which yields addresses with statistically different lifetimes and a maximum of three concurrent temporary addresses with the default values. DESYNC_FACTOR is a random value in the range 0 to MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR, computed each time an address is generated and associated with it, which must be smaller than TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus REGEN_ADVANCE. TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES has a default value of 3.

This document revises RFC 4941. It addresses flaws in the earlier algorithm, including the use of MD5 and the reuse of the same identifier for multiple prefixes. It allows hosts to employ only temporary addresses, because it no longer implies or requires the configuration of stable addresses. It removes the recommendation that temporary addresses be disabled by default. It reduces TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME from 1 week to 2 days, which decreases the typical number of concurrent temporary addresses from 7 to 3. DESYNC_FACTOR is computed each time an address is generated so that addresses are not generated at any specific frequency, and the requirement not to try again after TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES consecutive DAD failures is relaxed from MUST NOT to SHOULD NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: The defaults give a temporary address one day of preferred use and two days of validity, with three addresses alive at once. A small random offset is added to each address so that hosts across the network do not all change at the same moment. Compared with the version it replaces, the valid lifetime is shortened from one week to two days and the old MD5-based method is gone.

sections.title: The Cost of Changing Addresses
sections.content:
Protecting individual privacy can conflict with maintaining and debugging a network. When clients use addresses that change over time it becomes harder to track down and isolate operational problems, for example to tell from a packet trace whether the behaviour comes from one errant host or from several.

Using a large number of IPv6 addresses can have negative implications for network devices that keep an entry for each address in some data structure. Concurrent active use of multiple addresses increases Neighbor Discovery traffic if neighbor caches are not large enough to store all the addresses on the link, which affects performance and energy efficiency on networks where multicast is expensive. Some network-security devices might incorrectly infer IPv6 address forging if temporary addresses are regenerated at a high rate.

Some servers refuse communications from clients whose IP address cannot be mapped into a DNS name, performing a DNS PTR query and then an AAAA query to verify it maps back to the same address. Clients not properly registered in the DNS may therefore be unable to access some services, although a host's non-changing DNS name would itself be a constant identifier. Some applications may not behave robustly if an address becomes invalid while still in use, or if they open several sessions and expect them all to use the same address.

RFC 4941 used the same identifier for several prefixes, which let a host join only one solicited-node multicast group per set of temporary addresses. This document requires that all temporary addresses on a host be statistically different from each other, so a network with several prefixes makes a host join more multicast groups. A host might then have to set its network interface card to promiscuous mode, which can affect battery life and system performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Rotating addresses has costs. Routers keep records per address, so more addresses mean more Neighbor Discovery traffic. Servers that check the reverse DNS name of a client may refuse it. Applications that expect every session to use one address can misbehave. And because each prefix now gets its own identifier, a host joins more multicast groups than before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a very small number of hosts use a given prefix for extended periods of time, changing only the interface-identifier part of the address may not be sufficient to mitigate address-based correlation, since the prefix acts as a constant identifier. The procedures are most effective when the prefix is reasonably nonstatic or used by a fairly large number of hosts. If a temporary address is used in a session where the user authenticates, any notion of privacy for that address is compromised for the parties that receive the authentication information.

The method is believed to be ineffective against sophisticated forms of traffic analysis, and more advanced techniques such as onion routing may be needed to increase effectiveness. Ingress filtering is deployed to prevent the use of spoofed source addresses in distributed denial-of-service attacks. In a network with a large number of hosts, new temporary addresses are created at a fairly high rate, which might make it difficult for ingress and egress filtering to distinguish legitimately changing temporary addresses from spoofed source addresses, which are in-prefix. This can be addressed with access-control mechanisms on a per-address basis at the network ingress point, though that carries the costs described in Section 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the identifier does not help much on a network with only one device, because the prefix still identifies it, and it does not defeat careful analysis of traffic patterns. It can also make it harder for routers that filter forged addresses to tell a legitimate changing address from a spoofed one, which is why per-address access control at the edge of the network is the answer.

viz.caption: THE SIX PROPERTIES A TEMPORARY ADDRESS MUST HAVE

items.title: Used to start outgoing sessions
items.text: Typically employed for initiating outgoing sessions.

items.title: Short-lived
items.text: Used for hours to days, then deprecated but still usable for open connections.

items.title: Limited lifetime
items.text: A valid lifetime and a preferred lifetime, shortened further on privacy-meaningful events.

items.title: Statistically different lifetimes
items.text: Each address expires at a different moment, so hosts do not all change together.

items.title: One per prefix, distinct per interface
items.text: Different prefixes and different interfaces get different identifiers.

items.title: Unpredictable
items.text: Hard to predict the identifiers even with knowledge of the algorithm.
